tiger.claim: Tigers prefer prey of 60-250 kg (predator:prey about 1:1, as in other solitary felids); preference falls off for prey more than ~2x their mass unless it is vulnerable.
Among large prey (gaur) tigers select young individuals; with very large prey, vulnerable animals are favoured.
Solitary large carnivores kill competitors smaller than themselves (killer typically 2-5x the victim); a tiger picks on smaller predators, not larger ones.
Stalk-and-ambush cats rely on closing in unseen and a short final rush; prey that detects them and runs is mostly given up rather than coursed.

lion.claim: Lions prefer 190-550 kg prey; the right-skewed tail toward bigger prey comes from collective hunting, so a lone lion avoids prey much beyond ~3x its mass unless it is hurt.
Prey well below 190 kg sits under the lion's preferred range (warthog only in line with availability); among small options a lion leans to the larger one.
Lions are the main killers of spotted hyenas and routinely kill smaller carnivores; they go for predators smaller than themselves.
Stalk-and-ambush cats rely on closing in unseen and a short final rush; prey that detects them and runs is mostly given up rather than coursed.

lionpack.claim: Group hunting skews lion prey toward larger species (buffalo, giraffe); grouping carnivores kill larger victims than solitary ones, and male lions are capable buffalo hunters.
Lion preference peaks at 190-550 kg; beyond ~8x a lion's mass (megaherbivores) a pair of lions leans back to smaller prey unless it is hurt.
Male lions kill hyenas (adults and cubs) and steal their kills; a coalition goes for smaller predators.
Stalk-and-ambush cats rely on closing in unseen and a short final rush; prey that detects them and runs is mostly given up rather than coursed.

jaguar.claim: Jaguars prefer 45-85 kg prey (capybara, giant anteater) and avoid tapirs; selection follows abundance and herd size more than body size, so the size tilt is mild.
Jaguars significantly avoid carnivorans as prey; combined with the size rule for interspecific killing, a jaguar does not pick predators larger than itself.
Stalk-and-ambush cats rely on closing in unseen and a short final rush; prey that detects them and runs is mostly given up rather than coursed.

cougar.claim: Cougars live on deer and (males especially) elk and moose, prey 1-4x their own mass; temperate pumas specialise on larger prey.
Prey far beyond elk size (over ~6x the cat) is outside the cougar's recorded diet unless it is weakened.
Cougars are subordinate: wolves kill cougars and take their kills, black bears drive them off 72% of their kills; a cougar avoids larger predators.
73% of puma deer kills were at forest edges where the cat ambushes prey moving past; it does not course prey that has bolted.

leopard.claim: Leopards prefer 10-40 kg prey (optimum ~25 kg, about a third of their mass); preference drops for prey above ~40 kg unless it is hurt.
Leopards lose at least 21% of kills to hyenas and hoist kills to avoid them, and yield to lions and tigers; a leopard avoids other predators, the larger the more so.
Stalk-and-ambush cats rely on closing in unseen and a short final rush; prey that detects them and runs is mostly given up rather than coursed.

smilodon.claim: Smilodon's uniquely reinforced forelimbs held down large prey for the canine bite; its diet was horses, camels, bison and other mid-sized to large herbivores.
Dental microwear suggests Smilodon took slightly smaller prey than the American lion (open-habitat baby mammoths are attributed to Homotherium), so it leans away from giants.
A robust, short-limbed pin-and-stab killer; built to grapple, not to run prey down.

utahraptor.claim: Kirkland et al. proposed Utahraptor preyed on the iguanodonts of its fauna (much heavier than itself); the Stikes Quarry block holds iguanodonts with several raptors.
Dromaeosaur group finds read best as Komodo-dragon-like feeding scrambles: individuals converge on prey already under attack (an iguanodont stuck in quicksand drew several Utahraptors).

wolf.claim: Elk-hunting success needs 2-6 wolves and bison 9-13, and moose-hunting packs are larger than deer-hunting packs; a lone wolf avoids prey over ~4x its mass unless it is hurt or running.
Wolves select vulnerable prey (calves, old, weak individuals).
Coursing hunters: wolves test prey, attack individuals that run and usually leave prey that stands its ground.
Wolves generally relinquish kills to grizzly bears; a lone wolf does not take on predators larger than itself.

wolfpack.claim: Packs of ~4 are at the plateau of elk-hunting success (2-6 wolves); a pack commits to large prey up to ~10x a wolf's mass.
Bison are ~3x harder than elk and success only levels off at 9-13 wolves; a pack of four leans away from bison-sized and bigger prey unless it is hurt or running.
Wolves select vulnerable prey (calves, old, weak individuals).
Wolves test prey, attack the individual that runs, and usually leave prey that stands its ground.
Wolf packs kill cougars and take their kills, and kill grizzly cubs at carcasses; a pack goes for predators up to ~4x a wolf's mass, not adult bears.

wolfpack6.claim: Bison-hunting success keeps rising up to 9-13 wolves, and packs that hunt moose are larger than packs that hunt deer; a big pack commits to formidable prey.
Wolves select vulnerable prey (calves, old, weak individuals).
Wolves test prey, attack the individual that runs, and usually leave prey that stands its ground.
Grouping carnivores kill larger victims than solitary ones; wolf packs kill cougars and contest bears at carcasses.

hyena.claim: Over 75% of hyena hunts are by lone animals, even on wildebeest and topi ~3x their mass; only zebra are usually hunted in groups. A lone hyena avoids prey beyond ~3x its mass unless it is hurt.
Lions are the main killers of hyenas, and hyenas need to outnumber lions ~4:1 to take a kill; a lone hyena avoids larger predators.
Spotted hyenas scavenge and steal kills and favour easy, already-caught or weakened prey; they converge on prey others are fighting.
Hyenas are coursing hunters that run prey down; success rises with each added hunter up to three.

hyenapack.claim: Zebra (~4-5x a hyena's mass) are hunted in groups and success rises from one to three hunters; a clan commits to large prey.
Hyenas outnumbering lions ~4:1 drive female and subadult lions off kills and mob lions near their dens; a clan of four takes on predators.
Spotted hyenas steal kills and favour weakened or already-engaged prey.
Hyenas course prey over long chases; a running animal draws the clan.

grizzly.claim: Brown bears are major predators of newborn ungulates but kill adults much less often; a grizzly leans to smaller or weakened prey.
Bears contest wolves for carcasses and wolves usually relinquish kills to them; a grizzly goes for prey others are already fighting.
Grizzlies dominate wolves (and cougars) at carcasses; a grizzly does not shy from other predators.

polar.claim: Polar bears live mainly on ringed seals (~0.1-0.2x their mass), and pups made up at least half the seals killed in spring; preference falls off for prey above ~half the bear's mass unless it is hurt.
Polar bears kill walruses, but adults with tusks are much less vulnerable than subadults or animals trapped at holes; large prey is taken when vulnerable.
Polar bears hunt seals by still-hunting at breathing holes and stalking, not long chases.

blackbear.claim: Black bears are major predators of newborn ungulates (fawns, calves) and rarely kill adults; preference falls off for prey near or above its mass unless it is hurt.
Black bears are the commonest scavenger of puma kills and pumas abandon 72% of kills once a bear finds them; a black bear goes for prey others are fighting.
Interspecific killing runs from larger to smaller carnivores; a black bear pushes around smaller predators (pumas) but not larger ones.
As an opportunistic predator it takes the easiest animals available.

honeybadger.claim: Startled honey badgers charge the attacker, raise hackles and release scent, which usually drives predators off; they also eat venomous snakes.

shortface.claim: Arctodus has been argued (Matheus 1995, a hypothesis) to use its size to take kills from wolves and sabre-toothed cats.
Craniodental morphometrics make Arctodus a colossal omnivore, not a fast-running super-predator; it takes weakened animals rather than coursing.

elephant.claim: Family groups respond to lion roars by bunching and mobbing toward the threat; older matriarchs lead the defensive approach.
Elephants form coalitions and protect group members that are being harassed or attacked (35 years of Amboseli field records).

mammoth.claim: Analogue (extinct; living proboscideans): elephant family groups bunch and mob predators; assumed for woolly mammoth herds, whose calves were taken by Homotherium (Friesenhahn Cave).
Analogue: elephants protect herd members under attack; assumed for mammoths.

gorilla.claim: A leading silverback charges perceived threats (human observers as predator surrogates; 106 and 33 charges) to protect infants, females and even unrelated immigrants; the leopard is the gorilla's only natural predator and males put themselves between attacker and group.
Silverbacks defend group members under attack (Tamura 2024); at Loango a silverback tried to defend his group against attacking chimpanzees.

The predators silverbacks face are leopard-sized; at Loango an outnumbered silverback was surrounded and chased off. Among predators it confronts ones up to about its own size rather than much larger ones.
Silverback threat displays are chest beats, roars and bluff charges that stop short: the aim is to drive the intruder off, not run it down.

walrus.claim: Adult walruses are aggressive and carry large tusks used in defence against polar bears; bears mostly take calves and sub-adults, rarely adults.
Adults defend vulnerable herd members (calves, sub-adults) a bear is attacking.
Walruses respond to bears on land by stampeding to the water (the main cause of stampedes on Wrangel Island); they don't run down a retreating animal.

giraffe.claim: Adult giraffes routinely survive lion attacks (claw marks on 13% of adults, mostly on hindquarters and flanks) and can injure or kill a lion with a kick; their weapon is aimed at predators.
A mother giraffe standing nearby drove off a lion attacking her calf by kicking at it.

ostrich.claim: The male guards the nest with his feet; eggs and chicks are lost to hyenas and jackals: the predators an ostrich stands and kicks are its size or smaller.
Its first defence is running; it stops predators with a kick when chicks need protecting or it can't flee.
Running is the first line of defence; the kick is a last resort, so it doesn't take on animals much bigger than itself unless they are hurt.

giantkangaroo.claim: Analogue (Procoptodon extinct; eastern grey kangaroo): large adult males are the only class that wards off dingo attacks (kicking, tail thumps, hopping toward and watching the dingo, a fight of over an hour); a dingo is ~0.2x a big male, so it squares up to smaller predators.
Large males flee shorter distances and ward off or take to water; defence is reactive, not pursuit.
